```{r, include = FALSE}
# the queries in this vignette use {dplyr}, and the graphs use {igraph},
# {tidygraph}, {sfnetworks} and {ggraph}, which gtfstools only suggests
has_dplyr <- requireNamespace("dplyr", quietly = TRUE)
has_igraph <- has_dplyr && requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)
has_viz <- has_dplyr &&
  requireNamespace("tidygraph", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("sfnetworks", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("ggraph", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = has_dplyr
)

Sys.setenv(OMP_THREAD_LIMIT = 2)
data.table::setDTthreads(2)

```

Many transport analyses, such as network centrality and transit assignment 
models, are carried out on a graph of the transit network rather than on 
its timetable. `build_graph()` builds such a graph from the trips of a
GTFS feed that depart within a period of day. The graph has two types of 
nodes:

- **stop** nodes, one per stop, the physical place where a passenger stands;
- **service** nodes, one for each route and direction at each stop it serves. 

obs. this way, a stop served by routes 1 and 2, both in one direction, gets 
*one stop node* and *two service nodes*, all at the same coordinates.

And four types of links:

- **in-vehicle** links between the service nodes of consecutive stops, with
  the mean travel time between them;
- **boarding** links from each stop to the service nodes from which trips
  depart, with the number of departures and the mean waiting time (half the
  headway);
- **alighting** links from each service node back to its stop;
- walking **transfer** links between nearby stops.

The graph can be returned as tables following the General Modeling Network
Specification (GMNS), or as an `{igraph}` or `{tidygraph}` graph. This vignette
shows how to build a transit network graph from GTFS feeds and how to analyse and plot the network with these packages like `{sfnetworks}` and `{ggraph}`. Please see the documentation of `build_graph()` for the details of how nodes and links are built.

# Preparing the feed

We will use the sample feed of Porto Alegre, included in the package, and build
the network of the morning peak, from 7am to 10am. `build_graph()` pools the
trips of every service in the feed. In this example, we will remove services running on weekends with `filter_by_weekday()`:

```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(gtfstools)
library(dplyr)

# read GTFS feed
path <- system.file("extdata/poa_gtfs.zip", package = "gtfstools")
gtfs <- read_gtfs(path)

# drop weekends
gtfs <- filter_by_weekday(
  gtfs,
  weekday = c("saturday", "sunday"), 
  keep = FALSE
  )
```

Oftentimes, a GTFS feed comes with a few inconsistencies, such as duplicated 
trips, unused stops, etc. This particular feed lists only the times of the 
first and the last stop of each trip, and the links between stops without times would have no travel time, so they couldn't be used to calculate travel times through the network. Here we will use the `fix_gtfs()` function to fix several 
of these inconsistencies. We also want to ensure that no trips exceed 25 km/h and that all trips have a minimum dwell time of 30 seconds to allow passengers to board and alight.

```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
gtfs <- fix_gtfs(gtfs, max_speed = 25, min_dwell_time = 30)
```

# Building a GMNS network

By default, `build_graph()` returns the GMNS `node`, `link` and `config`
tables:

```{r}
g_gmns <- build_graph(
  gtfs, 
  from = "07:00:00", 
  to = "10:00:00", 
  format = "gmns"
  )

head(g_gmns$node)

head(g_gmns$link)

g_gmns$link |>
  dplyr::count(link_type)
```

The tables can be written to the CSV files of a GMNS network with
`data.table::fwrite()`, as shown in the examples of `build_graph()`, and then
read by other modelling software.


# Building and igraph and Calculating the centrality of stops

With `format = "igraph"`, the network is returned as an `{igraph}` graph, whose
links have the travel time as an attribute. We use it to calculate the shortest
travel times between every pair of stops, which include the waiting time at
the stops where vehicles are boarded:

```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, eval = has_igraph}
library(igraph)

g_igraph <- build_graph(
  gtfs, 
  from = "07:00:00", 
  to = "10:00:00", 
  format = "igraph"
  )

# get stop nodes
stop_nodes <- igraph::V(g_igraph)[node_type == "stop"]

# get travel times between stops
travel_times <- igraph::distances(
  g_igraph,
  v = stop_nodes,
  to = stop_nodes,
  mode = "out",
  weights = igraph::E(g_igraph)$travel_time
)

# travel time from one stop to itself is NA
# an `Inf` value means {igraph} found no path for a given origin-destination pair.
diag(travel_times) <- NA
```

From these travel times, we calculate the closeness centrality of each stop, 
which tell us how close a node is to all other nodes in the network. To do 
this, we calculate harmonic mean of the inverse of the travel times between each stop and the other stops. Stops that can't be reached count as 0. We don't use the centrality functions of `{igraph}`, such as `closeness()`, because they would also take the service nodes as destinations, and because they require positive weights,
while alighting links have a travel time of 0. This sample feed has a single
direction of each route, so the closeness *from* a stop depends on how far it
is from the end of its routes, and the closeness *to* it on how far it is from
their start. Hence we average the closeness from and to each stop:

```{r, eval = has_igraph}
closeness <- data.frame(
  stop_id = stop_nodes$stop_id,
  stop_name = stop_nodes$stop_name,
  closeness_from = rowMeans(1 / travel_times, na.rm = TRUE),
  closeness_to = colMeans(1 / travel_times, na.rm = TRUE)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(closeness = (closeness_from + closeness_to) / 2)

closeness |>
  dplyr::slice_max(closeness, n = 10)
```

# Plotting the network with tidygraph, sfnetworks and ggraph

With `format = "tidygraph"`, the network is returned as a `{tidygraph}` graph,
whose nodes have the coordinates of their stops. These coordinates can be used
to plot the network with `{ggraph}`:

```{r, eval = has_viz, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggraph)
library(tidygraph)
library(sfnetworks)

```

```{r, eval = has_viz, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, dpi = 96}
a <- build_graph(gtfs, from = "08:00:00", to = "10:00:00", format = "tidygraph")
a

ggraph(a, layout = "manual", x = x_coord, y = y_coord) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point()
```

This plot treats longitudes and latitudes as plain coordinates. To work with
the network as spatial data, we convert it into an `{sfnetworks}` network, in
which nodes are points and links are lines. Since boarding and alighting links
connect nodes at the same place, we keep only the in-vehicle and transfer
links, and place the in-vehicle links last, so that they are drawn on top:

```{r, eval = has_viz}
net <- a |>
  tidygraph::activate("edges") |>
  dplyr::filter(link_type %in% c("in_vehicle", "transfer")) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(link_type)) |>
  sfnetworks::as_sfnetwork(
    coords = c("x_coord", "y_coord"),
    crs = 4326,
    remove = FALSE,
    edges_as_lines = TRUE,
    message = FALSE
  )

net
```

`net` can be used with the functions of `{sfnetworks}` and `{sf}`, for
example to filter the network by a spatial extent or to join it with other
spatial data. It can also be mapped with the `"sf"` layout of `{ggraph}`:

```{r, eval = has_viz, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, dpi = 96}
ggraph(net, layout = "sf") +
  geom_edge_sf(aes(colour = link_type)) +
  geom_node_sf(size = 0.5) +
  scale_edge_colour_manual(
    name = "Link type",
    values = c(in_vehicle = "#0072B2", transfer = "#D55E00"),
    labels = c(in_vehicle = "In-vehicle", transfer = "Walking transfer")
  ) +
  theme_void()
```
